sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The main image and the headline don't make one idea together.** There is no main image. The right half of the navy hero, about x 820–1216 and y 62–462 (roughly 400 × 400 px), is a flat empty field. The headline promises to show "where every dollar goes this month", and nothing on the page shows it: no category breakdown, no budget bar, no alert. The viewer has to take the claim on trust.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the hero looks unfinished or broken, and the empty right side makes the composition feel lopsided.
   - **Why it matters:** a budgeting product's best argument is a look at the thing itself. This is common sense and taste; the catalog entry has no approved source.
   - **Fix direction:** fill the space with a visual that finishes the headline's idea. For example, a phone or panel showing one month's spending by category, with one category close to its limit and a "heads-up" alert. That shows the subhead's promise rather than repeating the headline's words.
   - **If the image just didn't load:** this is a capture problem, not a design flaw. Check the page in a live browser.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major.

**What's working.**
- **The copy is specific and speaks to the viewer.** The headline names a concrete outcome ("every dollar", "this month"). The subhead gives three verbs in order: connect, set a limit, get a heads-up. The "Read-only access" card ends on what the viewer cares about: the app "can never move money". The viewer doesn't have to piece together what the product does.
- **The navy and white match the job.** One dark field, plain sans-serif type and white buttons give a calm, trustworthy tone that suits an app asking for bank access. Type, color and shapes all feel like the same product.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Whether the empty hero area is a missing image.** If it's an image or animation that didn't load, Finding 1 is about the capture, not the design. Check in a live browser.
- **The blank white band at the bottom (about y 590–800).** It may just be where the screenshot was cut off, or it may be a real gap before the next section. Scroll the live page to see which.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea).

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the white headline "See where every dollar goes this month" (~56 px, 64–240 y). Then it drops to the white "Try it free" button (64,350), and then to the three bold feature headings at y≈509. It reads as a landing page for a consumer budgeting app. Clean, calm, a bit templated. Job (assumed): get people who manage a personal or household budget to start a free trial.

What matters first:
- One element stands clearly above the rest? **yes**. The headline is about 3× the next size, white on navy, and nothing else competes.
- Each text level distinct, no two sizes almost the same? **yes**. Headline ~56, subhead ~20, feature headings ~18 bold, body ~15 grey. The subhead (~20 regular, white on navy) and the feature headings (~18 bold, near-black on white) are close in size. Weight, colour and their separate bands tell them apart, so they don't read as a mistake.
- Headings differ from the text in more than size? **yes**. The feature headings are bold and near-black, and the body is regular and grey.

No line answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The headline clearly comes first. At about 56 px bold white on the navy band, it is roughly three times the size of anything else, so the eye has one obvious place to start and the product's promise is the first thing read.
- The levels are few, and each one is told apart in more than one way. Headline, subhead, feature heading and body each step down in size, and also in weight or colour: the feature headings are bold near-black over regular grey body at ~15 px. Each feature scans as a heading and then one sentence, with no level blurring into the next. Keep this when revising: don't add sizes between ~15 and ~20.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts because Bash is denied in this session. The image is 1280×800, one screen, so I judged it from the whole image and read the entries in `references/layout.md` directly.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. Everything in the navy hero (y 62–462) sits in its left 60%: the headline runs x 64–781, the subhead stops around x 658 and the buttons around x 386. The right part, about x 800–1280 by 400 px tall, is plain navy with nothing in it. The hero looks lopsided, and the empty block reads as a picture or product screenshot that never loaded, not as space left on purpose. Nothing on the right outweighs the large white headline. The page also gives up the one spot where it could show the product, so "See where every dollar goes" is a promise the visitor has to take on trust. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight. Fix: put something in that space that weighs as much as the headline block and works on the grid's column 3 lines (x 859–1216), such as a screenshot of a category budget with its limit warning. If a picture is supposed to be there and didn't load, this finding goes away. If the space is meant to be empty, make the text block wider or more open so the hero stops looking like it is missing half. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- One grid runs down the page. The logo, headline, subhead, buttons and first feature column all start at x≈64. The three feature columns repeat at an even pitch of about 397 px (x 64 / 461 / 859), and the nav ends at x 1216, which matches the 64 px margin on the left. Nothing almost lines up and misses, so the page looks built rather than placed by eye. Keep this grid when filling the right side of the hero.
- The spacing shows what belongs together. Each feature heading sits about 10 px above its own text, with much more space between columns and about 47 px between the hero and the feature row. Inside the hero, the steps from headline to subhead to buttons are clear. Every group reads at a glance.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The white band from about y 575 to 800 under the feature row is empty. It is probably where the page ends or where the screenshot stopped, not a design choice. Check in a live browser that the next section follows at a normal gap. If the page really ends here, the feature row is left floating on blank space.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances)

First read: the eye goes straight to the big white headline on navy, then to the "Try it free" button, then down to the three feature headings. It's a landing page for a budgeting app. It feels calm and plain, maybe a bit generic.

Job (assumed): a marketing landing page that gets people who manage household money to sign up.

Walk, Text section:
- Body text large enough, not smaller than menu/button text: yes (feature text is about 15 px, the same as the nav)
- Captions/labels large enough: yes
- Paragraphs in a plain upright face: yes
- One typeface plan: yes (one sans family)
- Small text weight holds up: yes
- Plain-background contrast: yes (feature body is dark grey on white and nav grey looks fine in the crop; white on navy is strong)
- Text over photo/gradient: yes (there is none; the navy is flat)
- Line length 45–75: yes (subhead about 65 characters, feature lines about 45–50)
- Leading suits the measure: yes
- Multi-line heading tight: yes
- Paragraphs flush left: yes
- Justified text: yes (there is none)
- Rag: yes
- Widows/runts: yes
- Heading breaks at phrases: yes ("goes / this month")
- Paragraph marks: yes
- Left edges crisp: yes
- Long text chunked: yes
- Mixed case: yes
- Emphasis one change: yes
- Large headings tighter: yes
- Kerning in display: yes
- Lower-case tracking: yes
- Caps letterspaced: yes (there are none)
- fi/fl ligatures: yes (no fi or fl in the large type)
- Real cuts: yes
- Quotes/dashes: yes (only hyphens in compound words)
- Tabular figures: yes (there are none)
- Real type: yes (looks like live text)
- No clipped text: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 is not needed.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The hero headline is set tightly.** "See where every dollar goes / this month" is large, bold and closely spaced, with tight leading. The two lines read as one unit, and the break falls at a phrase, so the promise lands in a single glance.
- **The text is easy to read at every size.** The hero subhead runs about 65 characters a line and the feature blurbs about 45–50. Both have comfortable leading. The feature body is a dark grey that stays clearly readable on white, not the washed-out grey that often comes with this template look.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes): Color**

First read: the eye lands on the big white headline on the navy band, then goes to the white "Try it free" button. It reads as a fintech landing page for a budgeting app: calm, trustworthy, plain. Job (assumed): get people who manage their own money to start a free trial.

1. Small palette: yes. Navy, white, and a near-black/gray text range, nothing else.
2. Strong colour kept to a small share: yes. The navy band is about half the screen, but it is a dark, muted navy rather than a saturated hue.
3. Clear light-dark range: yes. Dark band against white page, white type on navy, dark type on white. The layout would read the same in grayscale.
4. Warm forward, cool back: yes. Everything is cool. The primary button comes forward through value (solid white on navy), not hue, and nothing warm is misplaced.
5. Matching colours look the same: yes. The navy label on "Try it free" matches the band.
6. No vibrating edges: yes.
7. Status colours used only for their meaning: yes, there are none.
8. Meaning not shown by colour alone: yes. Primary and secondary buttons differ by fill against outline, not just hue.
9. Dark theme background not pure black: yes. Not a dark theme, and the navy band is not black anyway.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One hue, used with restraint.** The single dark navy against white and gray reads as calm and trustworthy, which suits a product that connects to bank accounts. Nothing on the page competes with it.
- **Value does the work instead of an accent colour.** The primary button "Try it free" is solid white on the navy band (about x 64–196, y 350–404), and "Watch the tour" is only an outline. So which button comes first is clear from lightness alone, and it holds up in grayscale and for colour-blind viewers. Keep that if an accent colour is added later.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes). The image is one screen, about 1280×800, so no crops are needed. The crop and entries scripts can't run because Bash is denied here.

First read: the eye lands on the white headline on navy, then drops to the solid white "Try it free" button. This is a landing page for a budgeting app. It's clean and generic. The bottom ~220 px are empty white.

Interface:
1. One primary action: yes. The filled white "Try it free" sits above the outlined "Watch the tour".
2. Controls look like what they do: yes.
3. Non-text contrast 3:1: yes. The white outline on navy is strong.
4. States: yes. None are shown.
5. Focus indicator: unsure, can't tell from a still.
6. Focus not obscured: unsure. Can't tell whether the header is sticky.
7. Main content uncovered: yes.
8. Target size: yes. Buttons look about 54 px tall. The nav links are small text but widely spaced.
9. Phone layout: yes (n/a).
10. Where the user is: yes. This is the home page.
11–21: yes (n/a: no dialogs, forms, destructive actions, empty states or errors).
22–23: yes (n/a).
24. Shortcuts: yes (n/a for a marketing page).
25. Anticipation: yes.
26. Conventions: no. The header has no sign-up action, and "Sign in" (x≈1168–1216, y≈31) has the same style and spacing as the page links.
27–32: yes.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has two hero buttons and a four-link header nav.

**Findings**
1. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?** In the header, "Sign in" (about x 1168–1216, y 31) has the same grey 15 px text and the same ~28 px gap as "Features", "Pricing" and "Security". The header also has no sign-up or "Try it free" action.
   - **What the viewer meets:** a returning user has to read all four links to find the account entry, because it looks like one more content page. A new user who scrolls past the hero (which ends at y 462) loses the only way to start. On most SaaS landing pages (Jakob's law, Nielsen Norman Group), account actions sit apart at the right end of the header, and the main action is repeated there as a small button.
   - **Fix:** set "Sign in" apart from the page links with a bigger gap or a divider. Add a compact primary button next to it that repeats the hero's "Try it free". I couldn't open the catalog entries ("Jakob's law", "Platform conventions") in this session, so this rests on the general convention.
   - Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **The two hero buttons have a clear order.** "Try it free" is solid white with navy text and "Watch the tour" is only outlined, so the primary action wins without the secondary one vanishing. The white outline on navy is far above 3:1, so the secondary button still clearly reads as a button.
- **The targets are generous.** The hero buttons look about 54 px tall with a 16 px gap between them. The nav links are small text but spaced about 28 px apart, so they're easy to hit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the buttons and nav links have a visible focus ring on navy and on white. Whether the header stays fixed on scroll and covers focused controls. Whether "Watch the tour" opens a video player that has a visible close control.

**Checklist.** `Interface: 32 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (navigation follows known conventions), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)`
